name: BerkeleyDB
listed_description: Library for a high-performance embedded database for key-value data.
reason: No verifiable numeric win over a named baseline. Oracle's own SQLite-comparison whitepaper (oracle.com bdb-sqlite-comparison-wp-176431.pdf) and the Oracle SQL API article returned HTTP 403, so the claimed figures (search-result summary only: about as fast as SQLite for reads, about 3x on updates) could not be read from a page I opened. The community fork archive (berkeleydb/libdb, Sleepycat license; Oracle 6.x+ is AGPL-3.0) only reports improvement against its own earlier code (shared-handle random reads 174k to 3.7M ops/s at 24 threads on 96 vCPUs) and its test/bench/CROSS-ENGINE-2026-09.md study shows libdb 5.3.37 behind WiredTiger by 4.5x to 58x; the regression harness README itself disclaims any absolute comparison with InnoDB, WiredTiger or LMDB. The LMDB microbench (lmdb.tech) that would show BDB as the slower engine is blocked.

name: FlashDB
listed_description: An ultra-lightweight database that supports key-value and time series data.
reason: README and docs give only absolute numbers on its own hardware (TSDB append 4 ms per record and query 1.77 ms on W25Q64 NOR flash; 0.37 ms and 0.11 ms on STM32F2 on-chip flash; code footprint about 4.6 KB for KVDB, 1.2 KB for TSDB on STM32F4 with IAR 8.20). No SQLite, EasyFlash, LittleFS or any other named baseline is measured anywhere in the repository README or docs/ pages, and a web search found no third-party comparison with numbers.

name: libmongoc
reason: The repo README makes no speed comparison. The companion repo mongodb/mongo-c-driver-performance only implements MongoDB's standard driver benchmark suite and prints bytes per second for libbson/libmongoc tests with no baseline column; searches for a cross-driver comparison (Python, Go, Java drivers) found only Jira tickets and forum threads without published numbers.
